etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English preventen (“anticipate”), from Latin praeventus, perfect passive participle of praeveniō (“I anticipate”), from prae (“before”) + veniō (“I come”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To stop (an outcome); to keep from (doing something). [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 2011 October 1, Tom Fordyce, “Rugby World Cup 2011: England 16-12 Scotland”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: Scotland must now hope Georgia produce a huge upset and beat Argentina by at least eight points in Sunday's final Pool B match to prevent them failing to make the last eight for the first time in World Cup history.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, now rare) To take preventative measures. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1897 October 16, Henry James, What Maisie Knew, Chicago, Ill., New York, N.Y.: Herbert S. Stone & Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: I think you must be mad, and she shall not have a glimpse of it while I'm here to prevent!

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To come before; to precede. [16th–18th c.]

quote.citation: 1549 March 7, Thomas Cranmer [et al.], compilers, The Booke of the Common Prayer and Administration of the Sacramentes, […], London:  […]  Edowardi Whitchurche […], →OCLC:
quote.text: We pray thee that thy grace may always prevent and follow us.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Thessalonians 4:15:
quote.text: We which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep.

quote.citation: 1718, Mat[thew] Prior, “Solomon on the Vanity of the World. A Poem in Three Books.”, in Poems on Several Occasions, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], and John Barber […], →OCLC, book II (Pleasure), page 448:
quote.text: Then had I come, preventing Sheba's Queen, / To ſee the comelieſt of the Sons of Men;  […]

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], part II (books IV–VI), London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC:
quote.text: With that he put his spurres vnto his steed, / With speare in rest, and toward him did fare, / Like shaft out of a bow preuenting speed.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To be beforehand with; to anticipate.

quote.citation: c. 1699 – 1703, Alexander Pope, “The First Book of Statius His Thebais”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], published 1717, →OCLC:
quote.text: their ready guilt preventing thy commands
